metadata.title: Teacher policies and teacher labor market outcomes: Results from cross-national comparison

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher and school data collected via a two-stage stratified cluster sampling design (schools sampled within countries; teachers sampled within schools). In the within-country two-level models, the authors explicitly apply teacher-level weights (tchwgt) and school-level weights (schwgt) from the TALIS dataset to correct for unequal selection probabilities across the two sampling stages and for varied response rates. The analysis then extracts adjusted country means from these weighted two-level models and uses them as system-level inputs for subsequent ANOVA/ANCOVA in SPSS 29. Replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are not mentioned, so uncertainty estimation is not specified at the replicate level in the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are TALIS questionnaire-based latent factor scores (extracted via an ESEM measurement model) and an observed intention-to-quit item, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. As a result, plausible values are not part of the analysis pipeline. The manuscript text provided does not describe how missing questionnaire responses were handled (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap because missingness can affect factor score estimation and country mean comparisons.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The authors start from the 48 lower-secondary participating countries in TALIS 2018 and then select a theoretically classified subset of 16 countries based on the Voisin and Dumay (2020) typology of teacher profession regulation models (Market, Bureaucratic, Training, Professional skills). The analytic sample comprises 53,178 teachers working in 3,076 schools across these 16 countries. For the intention-to-quit dependent variable (TT3G50), they further restrict the sample to teachers with less than or equal to 25 years of seniority to reduce confounding from higher end-of-career propensity to leave.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (lower secondary, teacher questionnaire) — 16-country cross-national comparison
main_findings.target_variable: Value of the profession (latent factor score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ANOVA/ANCOVA results: F=3.958*; R square=0.497 (Table 5). Bureaucratic model shows lower adjusted value than Market and Professional skills; effect remains significant after controlling for economic status (Table 6) and individualism (Table 7).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (lower secondary teacher questionnaire) data for 16 theoretically selected countries, the study leveraged teacher and school covariates (e.g., teacher gender and effective professional development) together with country-level confounders (economic status of teaching and individualism) to compare adjusted country means of the value of the profession, finding that the Bureaucratic regulation model is associated with a substantially lower perceived value than the Market and Professional skills models (F=3.958, R²=0.497). This indicates that policy systems characterized by bureaucratic rules and limited career advancement may undermine teachers’ perceived occupational value even when job security is high, suggesting that reforms should address non-monetary career and valuation mechanisms rather than focusing only on employment protection.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (lower secondary, teacher questionnaire) — 16-country cross-national comparison
main_findings.target_variable: Satisfaction with employment conditions (latent factor score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ANOVA/ANCOVA results: F=3.928*; R square=0.495 (Table 5). Bureaucratic model shows lower satisfaction with employment than Market and Professional skills; effect remains significant after controlling for economic status (Table 6) and is largely confirmed with individualism (Table 7).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (lower secondary teacher questionnaire) data for 16 countries, the study leveraged teacher and school covariates (including employment status and disciplinary climate) and country-level confounders (economic status of teaching and individualism) to compare adjusted satisfaction with employment conditions, finding that the Bureaucratic regulation model is associated with lower employment-condition satisfaction than the Market and Professional skills models (F=3.928, R²=0.495). This indicates that bureaucratic regulation may reduce perceived employment quality through aspects beyond salary and security, implying that policy attention should extend to career progression, professional autonomy, and the lived experience of employment conditions.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (lower secondary, teacher questionnaire) — 16-country cross-national comparison
main_findings.target_variable: Satisfaction with the profession (latent factor score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ANOVA/ANCOVA results: F=2.228 (Table 5) with R square=0.363; not significant as a main effect in Table 5. Two-by-two differences indicate Professional skills teachers are less satisfied with the profession than Market teachers (reported in Results text).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (lower secondary teacher questionnaire) data for 16 countries, the study leveraged teacher and school covariates (such as teaching as career choice and school leadership) and country-level confounders to compare adjusted satisfaction with the profession, finding that overall regulation-model differences are not significant in the main ANOVA (F=2.228, R²=0.363) but that two-by-two comparisons show lower satisfaction in the Professional skills model relative to the Market model. This indicates that professional skills systems may generate dissatisfaction with the profession itself even when economic and cultural confounders are considered, suggesting that teacher support and workload/stress management should accompany professionalization and accountability reforms.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (lower secondary, teacher questionnaire) — 16-country cross-national comparison
main_findings.target_variable: Satisfaction with the work environment (latent factor score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ANOVA/ANCOVA results: F=18.849**; R square=0.825 (Table 5). Professional skills model shows lower satisfaction with work environment than other models; effect remains significant after controlling for economic status (Table 6) and individualism (Table 7), though regional controls mitigate the pattern (Tables 8-9).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (lower secondary teacher questionnaire) data for 16 countries, the study leveraged school-level factors (e.g., team innovativeness and teacher-student relations) and country-level confounders (economic status and individualism) to compare adjusted satisfaction with the work environment, finding a very large and significant regulation-model effect with the Professional skills model associated with substantially lower work-environment satisfaction (F=18.849, R²=0.825). This indicates that professional skills regulation—often combining professional development with performance-driven monitoring—may impose psychological or organizational pressure on teachers, implying that policy design should include safeguards for working conditions and stress-related risks.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (lower secondary, teacher questionnaire) — 16-country cross-national comparison (restricted to ≤25 years seniority)
main_findings.target_variable: Intention to quit within 5 years (observed item TT3G50)
main_findings.performance_metrics: ANOVA/ANCOVA results: F=1.704 (Table 5) with R square=0.317 (not significant in main ANOVA). ANCOVA indicates a significant effect after controlling for economic status, with higher intention to leave in the Market model than in the Bureaucratic model (reported in Results text).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (lower secondary teacher questionnaire) data for 16 countries, with the intention-to-quit outcome restricted to teachers with ≤25 years seniority, the study leveraged teacher experience and mobility covariates together with country-level confounders to compare adjusted intention to quit, finding that the main ANOVA does not show a significant regulation-model effect (F=1.704, R²=0.317) but that ANCOVA reveals higher intention to leave in the Market model than in the Bureaucratic model after controlling for economic status. This indicates that market-oriented regulation may increase attrition intentions through labor-market permeability and accountability pressures, suggesting that retention strategies should target working-condition stressors and mobility pathways rather than relying solely on compensation.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 lower-secondary teacher questionnaire data from 16 cross-nationally selected countries (53,178 teachers in 3,076 schools) to examine how four typological models of teacher profession regulation (Market, Bureaucratic, Training, Professional skills) relate to teachers’ perceived value of the profession, satisfaction with employment conditions, satisfaction with the profession, satisfaction with the work environment, and intention to quit within 5 years. The authors estimate within-country two-level models using TALIS teacher and school weights (tchwgt and schwgt), extract adjusted country means, and then compare regulation models via ANOVA/ANCOVA in SPSS 29. Key results include a strong regulation effect on work-environment satisfaction (F=18.849, R²=0.825) with the Professional skills model showing lower satisfaction, and significant effects on perceived value and employment-condition satisfaction (F≈3.9, R²≈0.49). The intention-to-quit outcome is restricted to teachers with ≤25 years seniority; main ANOVA is not significant (F=1.704) but ANCOVA indicates higher quitting intentions in the Market model than the Bureaucratic model after controlling for economic status. Limitations include reliance on subjective TALIS measures and the absence of any ML modeling (no predictive algorithms), so findings are about statistical associations rather than causal effects.
